newsitem.title: MALDIVES: India, Pakistan in highest-level talks in 4 years.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan in highest-level talks in 4 years.

text.p: The prime ministers of India and Pakistan meet this week in the highest-level meeting between the arch-rivals in four years, but diplomats cautioned against expectations of a breakthrough in the peace talks.
Pakistani Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif and his Indian counterpart, Inder Kumar Gujral, were to hold their first face-to-face talks on Monday at a resort on this Indian Ocean island nation.
The meeting will be held on the sidelines of a summit meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC).
Sharif was named prime minister in February and Gujral took office three weeks ago. They have exchanged letters expressing their hope that the two longtime rivals could ease tensions.

But Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan on Saturday played down the prospects of a quick breakthrough in peace talks with, saying there could be setbacks and negotiations would take a long time.
"Expectations should not be built up because unless the groundwork is there, there could be disappointments," Khan said.

Khan said it would be a long, drawn-out negotiation between the two countries over the divided region of Kashmir, the cause of two of the three wars the neighbours have fought since independence in 1947.

The two states launched bilateral negotiations in March after a three-year hiatus marked by tension over Kashmir, where police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have died in a separatist insurgency.

The two nations' foreign secretaries -- the senior-most civil servants in the foreign ministries -- met in March, followed by talks last month between Khan and Gujral, who was foreign minister before being elevated to prime minister.
"Good relations between Pakistan and India are essential for both the countries," Pakistani analyst Samina Ahmed said, but added that the dispute over the Himalayan region was equally important.
The meeting between Gujral and Sharif will be the first face-to-face encounter between the nations' prime ministers since April 1993.
Negotiations bogged down in January over Kashmir, two-thirds of which is ruled by India and the rest by Pakistan.
New Delhi, which is fighting a separatist revolt in its part of Kashmir, regards the region as an integral part of the Indian union.

But Islamabad, which denies New Delhi's charges of training and arming the rebels, wants the mainly Moslem Kashmiris to be allowed to vote in a U.N.-mandated plebiscite whether to join Islamic Pakistan or Hindu-majority India.

No agenda has been announced for the talks that many diplomats and analysts said may yield little by way of concrete results but could lead to meeting of foreign secretaries of the two countries in Islamabad, probably next month.

Pakistan insists that Kashmir is the "core issue" and must be on the agenda of any India-Pakistan dialogue. India has balked at putting the issue on the table but has said all matters are up for negotiation now.
Samina Ahmed, a research analyst at the Islamabad-based Institute of Regional Studies, said the very fact the two prime ministers were meeting was significant.
"I think the very fact that you have add the resumption of diplomatic negotiations between India and Pakistan is symbolically very promising because you are saying that we are willing to talk again."
A Pakistan-based economist, Ishfaq Hassan, said the meeting might not lead to any significant easing of tension.
"I do not expect much out of the bilateral meeting. The maximum is that they might ease visa restrictions. They might discuss opening of consulate office in Karachi," he said.
